prompt: `func double(n int) { n = n * 2 }` is called as `double(n)` with `n := 21`. What does `n` hold afterwards?
hint: Whose variable did the function double?

choices.text: 42, because the function doubled it
choices.why: It doubled its own `n`, a variable made for the call. The caller's `n` was never handed over.

choices.text: Nothing: assigning to a parameter is a compile error
choices.why: A parameter is an ordinary local variable, and `double` compiled and ran in section 02.

choices.text: 21, because the function doubled a copy of it
choices.why: Right. The call copied 21 into the function's own `n`; the first line of output was 21.

choices.text: 0, since a parameter is reset when the function returns
choices.why: Nothing resets the caller's variable; it keeps the 21 it had, because only its value left it.

prompt: `Player` has a field `Last [3]int`. After `bia := ana` and `bia.Last[1] = 50`, what is `ana.Last`?
hint: Is an array field part of the struct, or somewhere else?

choices.text: `[0 50 0]`, because the two structs share their array
choices.why: That would be true of a slice field. An array field is inside the struct and was copied with it.
Right. Copying a struct copied its array, so writing into `bia`'s left `ana`'s alone.
`bia.Last[1] = 50` writes one element, and of `bia`'s array at that.

choices.text: A compile error, since a struct holding an array cannot be assigned
choices.why: `bia := ana` compiled in section 02; a struct is assigned whole whatever its fields are.

prompt: A parameter is an ordinary local ___ that the call fills in with a copy of the argument.
hint: The function can read it, change it and throw it away.

prompt: `win(p Player) Player` changes `p.Score` and returns `p`; the caller writes `ana = win(ana)`. What does this shape give the reader of the call?
hint: Look at the left-hand side of the call.

choices.text: It saves the copy that passing `ana` would cost
choices.why: It makes three copies, not fewer: into `p`, out as the result, and into `ana`.

choices.text: Nothing extra: it is the one way Go lets a function change a value for its caller
choices.why: There is a second way, passing the address, which lesson 23 is about.

choices.text: The assignment shows, at the call, that `ana` changes
choices.why: Right. Nobody has to open `win` to know `ana` is replaced.

choices.text: It makes `win` run faster than a function that returns no value
choices.why: Returning a value adds a copy; the benefit is legibility, not speed.

prompt: A function receives `players []Player` and runs `for _, p := range players { p.Score = 0 }`. What happens to the caller's players?
hint: What is `p` on each turn of the loop?

choices.text: Every score becomes 0, as the array is shared
choices.why: The array is shared, but the loop never writes into it: it writes into `p`.

choices.text: Nothing: `p` is a copy of each element, and the loop changes the copy
choices.why: Right. `range` hands over a copy of each element, the same copy a call makes; `players[i].Score = 0` would reach the array.

choices.text: Only the first player changes, since the copy is made once
choices.why: A copy is made on every turn, and none of them is the element.

choices.text: It does not compile, because `p` cannot be assigned to
choices.why: `p` is an ordinary variable and assigning to its field compiles; it just changes nothing outside.

prompt: On the lab's machine, how many bytes does `unsafe.Sizeof` report for a variable of type `map[string]int` that holds a million keys?
hint: What does a map variable hold?

prompt: `replace(m map[string]int)` runs `m = map[string]int{"carla": 3}`. The caller passed `ages`, holding `ana` and `bia`. What does the caller's `ages` hold afterwards?
hint: Did the function write through the pointer, or replace it?

choices.text: `carla` alone, because maps are passed by reference
choices.why: That is what pass by reference would do, and the program printed the opposite.

choices.text: `ana`, `bia` and `carla`, because both maps merge
choices.why: Nothing merges maps; `carla` went into a new table only `m` pointed at.

choices.text: Nothing: `ages` is nil after the call
choices.why: The caller's variable was not touched at all, so it still points at its table.

choices.text: `ana` and `bia`, as before the call
choices.why: Right. The assignment changed `m`, the function's copy of the pointer, and nothing else.

prompt: `load(m map[string]int)` does `if m == nil { m = make(map[string]int) }` and adds a key. The caller declared `var ages map[string]int`, called `load(ages)`, then wrote `ages["bia"] = 2` and the program panicked. Why?
hint: Which variable did `make` go into?

choices.text: `load` emptied the map when it returned
choices.why: Returning empties nothing; the map `load` made was simply never stored where the caller looks.

choices.text: The new map went into `load`'s own variable, and `ages` stayed nil
choices.why: Right. The program printed `true` for `ages == nil`, and writing to a nil map panics.

choices.text: Maps made inside a function are freed when it returns
choices.why: A map lives as long as something points at it; nothing in `main` did.

choices.text: A map has to be made with `make` in the same function that writes to it
choices.why: The fixed `load` made the map and `main` wrote to it, once the map was returned.

prompt: Match each type with what a copy of its value shares with the original.
hint: Section 03's table, the last column.

pairs.right: the elements of an array, but not the length
the whole table, keys added through either copy included
a struct copied in when it was stored

right_distractors: the caller's variable itself, which it renames

prompt: `var v any = ana` stores a `Player` whose score is 10; then `ana.Score = 99`. What does `fmt.Println(v)` print?
hint: An interface value is two words. What does the second point at?

choices.text: `{Ana 99}`, because an interface points at the variable it was given
choices.why: It points at a stored value, and the stored value was a copy taken at `v = ana`.
Right. Storing a struct in an interface copied it; the run printed `{Ana 10} {Ana 99}`.

choices.text: `<nil>`, since `any` holds no fields
choices.why: `any` holds whatever was stored in it, fields and all.

choices.text: Nothing: assigning a struct to `any` does not compile
choices.why: Every type satisfies `any`, so the assignment compiles; lesson 28 is about it.

prompt: A function receives `m map[string]int`. Which of these does the caller see after the function returns? Choose all that apply.
hint: Through the pointer, or to the pointer?

choices.why: Yes: it writes into the table both copies point at.

choices.text: `delete(m, "ana")`
choices.why: Yes: deleting goes through the pointer to the same table, like adding.

choices.text: `m = map[string]int{}`
choices.why: No: that changes which table `m` points at, and `m` is the function's own copy.

choices.text: `m = nil`
choices.why: No: the caller's variable keeps its pointer whatever the function assigns to `m`.

prompt: A function only needs to read a few elements of a `[1_000_000]int`. What is the usual way to stop every call copying 8,000,000 bytes?
hint: What did `viaSlice` take?

choices.text: Declare the array as a global variable and stop passing it
choices.why: That avoids the copy by making every function depend on one variable, which is a different problem.

choices.text: Mark the function `//go:noinline`
choices.why: That directive stops inlining, which keeps the copy; the benchmark used it so the copy would be measured.

choices.text: Pass a slice over the array, 24 bytes
choices.why: Right. The slice took 2.026 ns where the array took 350,746 ns, and it shares the elements.

choices.text: Split it into a thousand smaller arrays
choices.why: Passing all of them would still copy every byte; the size of the copy is the problem.

prompt: `Point` (16 bytes) took 1.954 ns per call and `Record` (1,024 bytes) took 15.51 ns. What does the pair show?
hint: Compare the ratio of bytes with the ratio of times.

choices.text: The cost grows with the bytes, and both are small next to the 8 MB array
choices.why: Right. Sixty-four times the bytes cost about eight times the time, and both stay in nanoseconds.

choices.text: Any struct over 16 bytes must be passed by pointer
choices.why: 15.51 ns is nothing a program notices outside a very hot loop; the section says to pass small structs by value.

choices.text: Copying is free, since both are under a microsecond
choices.why: The array line shows it is not: 350,746 ns for one copy.

choices.text: The time is the cost of the call alone, which is the same whatever the size
choices.why: The times differ with the size; only at 16 or 24 bytes is the call the whole cost.

prompt: Why does each measured function in `~/byvalue-cost` carry `//go:noinline`?
hint: What would the compiler do with a one-line function otherwise?

choices.text: It is a comment for the reader, ignored by the compiler
choices.why: With no space after the slashes it is a directive the compiler obeys.

choices.text: `testing.Benchmark` refuses to time a function without it
choices.why: `testing.Benchmark` times whatever its function does; the directive is about the compiler.

choices.text: It makes the copy faster, so the numbers come out smaller
choices.why: It keeps the copy exactly as it is; that is the point.

choices.text: So the call, and the copy it makes, is not pasted into the loop and optimised away
choices.why: Right. An inlined one-line function lets the compiler skip the copy that was being timed.

prompt: A colleague changes every function that takes a three-field `Customer` struct to take a pointer instead, "for speed". What does this lesson's measurement say about that?
hint: Where does a three-field struct sit in the table?

choices.text: It is right: a pointer is 8 bytes, so each call becomes about twice as fast
choices.why: At this size the time is the call's, not the copy's, so halving the bytes saves nearly nothing.

choices.text: It buys almost no time and gives up the copy that kept callers safe
choices.why: Right. A small struct copies at about the cost of the call, and lesson 24 shows a pointer has costs of its own.

choices.text: It changes nothing, because Go passes structs by pointer already
choices.why: Go copies a struct into the parameter; section 02 showed the caller's struct unchanged.

choices.text: It is required once a struct holds a string field
choices.why: A string field is 16 bytes and is copied like any other; nothing requires a pointer.

prompt: Put the copies in `ana = win(ana)` in the order they happen, where `win(p Player) Player` increments `p.Score` and returns `p`.
hint: The call comes before the body, and the assignment comes last.
items: `p` is copied out as the result

prompt: `func reset(s []int) { s = nil }` is called as `reset(nums)` with `nums` holding `[1 2 3]`. What is `nums` afterwards?
hint: It is `replace` from section 03, with a slice.

choices.text: `[]`, because a slice is passed by reference
choices.why: A slice is passed as a copy of its three words, and `s = nil` changed only the copy.
Right. Assigning to the parameter replaces the function's copy and leaves the caller's slice as it was.

choices.text: `[0 0 0]`, since the array is shared and `nil` zeroes it
choices.why: `nil` is not written into any element; it is a new value for `s` alone.

choices.text: A panic, because the array behind `nums` was freed
choices.why: `nums` still points at its array, so the array is alive and nothing panics.

prompt: `func zero(s []int) { for i := range s { s[i] = 0 } }` is called as `zero(nums)` with `nums` holding `[1 2 3]`. What is `nums` afterwards?
hint: This loop writes through `s[i]`, not into a loop variable.

choices.text: `[1 2 3]`, because Go passes everything to a function by value
choices.why: It does, and the value copied holds a pointer to the caller's array; writes through it land there.

choices.text: `[]`, since zeroing a slice empties it
choices.why: Writing zeros into elements keeps the length at 3.

choices.text: `[0 0 0]`, because `s[i]` writes into the array `nums` uses
choices.why: Right. The copy of the slice points at the same array, as lesson 11's `setFirst` showed.

choices.text: `[0 2 3]`, as only the first write reaches the caller
choices.why: Every `s[i]` goes through the same pointer, so every element is reached.

prompt: Each function changes its parameter as shown. Which of them change something the caller sees? Choose all that apply. (`Team` is `struct { Members []string }`.)
hint: Ask what each value points at.

choices.text: `func a(p Player) { p.Score = 0 }`
choices.why: No: `p` is a whole copy of the struct, and its fields point at nothing of the caller's.

choices.text: `func b(t Team) { t.Members[0] = "Bia" }`
choices.why: Yes: the struct was copied, and its slice field still points at the caller's array.

choices.text: `func c(a [3]int) { a[0] = 0 }`
choices.why: No: an array is copied element by element, as lesson 11 showed with `zero`.

choices.text: `func d(m map[string]int) { m["x"] = 1 }`
choices.why: Yes: the map value is a pointer to one table, and the key goes into it.

prompt: Go passes every argument by ___; for a map, what gets copied is a pointer to the table.
hint: The opposite of "by reference".
